questions.q: Which bony landmark on the femur receives the insertion of the iliopsoas muscle?
questions.explain: Iliopsoas (iliacus and psoas major) inserts onto the lesser trochanter on the posteromedial aspect of the proximal femur. The greater trochanter receives gluteus medius, gluteus minimus, and piriformis among others.

open.q: Onto which femoral prominence does the iliopsoas muscle insert?

questions.q: Which rough vertical ridge along the posterior aspect of the femoral shaft serves as a major attachment for thigh muscles and intermuscular septa?
questions.explain: The linea aspera is a prominent longitudinal ridge along the middle third of the posterior femoral shaft that gives attachment to vastus medialis, vastus lateralis, adductor muscles, and the short head of biceps femoris.

open.q: What is the prominent longitudinal ridge along the posterior shaft of the femur called?

questions.q: Which small depression on the head of the femur serves as the attachment site for the ligament of the head of the femur (ligamentum teres)?
questions.explain: The fovea capitis femoris is an unossified pit on the femoral head where the ligament of the head of the femur attaches, carrying a small artery to the femoral head in children.

open.q: What pit on the head of the femur attaches the ligament of the head of the femur?

questions.q: Which large bony projection on the proximal anterior tibia serves as the insertion site for the quadriceps femoris tendon via the patellar ligament?
questions.explain: The tibial tuberosity lies on the anterior proximal tibia and receives the patellar ligament, transmitting the pull of quadriceps femoris to extend the knee. In adolescents, traction here can cause Osgood-Schlatter disease.

open.q: Which proximal anterior tibial landmark receives the patellar ligament?

questions.q: Which bone of the leg is non-weight-bearing and forms the lateral malleolus of the ankle?
questions.explain: The fibula is slender and primarily serves for muscle attachment and ankle stabilization rather than major axial weight bearing, expanding distally as the lateral malleolus. The tibia is the main weight-bearing bone of the leg.

open.q: Which leg bone forms the lateral malleolus and bears little axial weight?

questions.q: Why is the neck of the fibula clinically important during fractures or trauma near the knee?
options: The femoral artery perforates the fibular neck
The common fibular (peroneal) nerve winds closely around the neck of the fibula
The sciatic nerve originates at the fibular neck
The achilles tendon inserts onto the fibular neck
questions.explain: The common fibular (peroneal) nerve passes around the lateral aspect of the neck of the fibula just beneath the skin and fascia, making it vulnerable to injury in fibular neck fractures or lateral knee trauma.

open.q: Why is injury to the common fibular nerve common with fractures of the fibular neck?
accept: the nerve winds closely around the fibular neck
common fibular nerve courses directly around the neck of the fibula
it wraps around the fibular neck superficially
the nerve lies immediately adjacent to the fibular neck

questions.q: Which tarsal bone is the largest and strongest bone of the foot and forms the prominence of the heel?
questions.explain: The calcaneus (heel bone) is the largest tarsal bone, forming the posterior pillar of the longitudinal arch and receiving the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon on its posterior surface.

open.q: Which tarsal bone forms the heel and receives the calcaneal tendon?

questions.q: Which tarsal bone articulates superiorly with the tibia and fibula at the ankle joint and transmits body weight to the calcaneus and navicular?
questions.explain: The talus sits superiorly in the ankle mortise formed by the tibia and fibula, articulating inferiorly with the calcaneus and anteriorly with the navicular. It has no muscular attachments and has a vulnerable blood supply to its body/neck.

open.q: Which tarsal bone articulates with the tibia and fibula to form the ankle joint?

questions.q: Which large gluteal muscle is the primary extensor of the thigh at the hip joint, especially during climbing stairs or rising from a seated position?
questions.explain: Gluteus maximus (innervated by the inferior gluteal nerve) is the chief extensor and lateral rotator of the thigh at the hip joint, inserting largely into the iliotibial tract and gluteal tuberosity.

open.q: Which gluteal muscle is the main extensor of the thigh at the hip joint?

questions.q: Why does paralysis of the left gluteus medius and gluteus minimus cause the pelvis to drop on the right side when standing on the left limb (positive Trendelenburg sign)?
options: Left abductors cannot flex the knee during stance
Left gluteus medius and minimus cannot keep the pelvis level
The left sciatic nerve prevents hip extension
questions.explain: During single-leg stance on the left limb, left gluteus medius and minimus (supplied by the superior gluteal nerve) contract to keep the pelvis level or tilted slightly toward the unsupported right side. If weakened, gravity pulls the unsupported right pelvis downward.

open.q: Why does weakness of the left gluteus medius and minimus cause the right side of the pelvis to sag during single-leg stance on the left?
accept: they cannot stabilize and level the pelvis against gravity on the stance side
loss of abductor pelvic stabilization during single-leg support
left hip abductors fail to hold the pelvis level
inability of left gluteus medius and minimus to support the pelvis

questions.q: Which nerve supplies gluteus medius, gluteus minimus, and tensor fasciae latae?
questions.explain: The superior gluteal nerve exits above piriformis through the greater sciatic foramen and innervates gluteus medius, gluteus minimus, and tensor fasciae latae.

open.q: Which nerve innervates gluteus medius, gluteus minimus, and tensor fasciae latae?

questions.q: A nurse administers an intramuscular injection into the inferomedial quadrant of the buttock and injures a large nerve emerging inferior to piriformis, causing weakness of knee flexion and distal leg/foot muscles. Which nerve was injured?
questions.explain: The sciatic nerve (L4 to S3) is the largest nerve in the body and typically exits the pelvis inferior to piriformis through the greater sciatic foramen. Giving injections in the superolateral quadrant helps avoid sciatic nerve injury.

open.q: Which large nerve emerges inferior to piriformis and is at risk during misplaced gluteal injections?

questions.q: Which nerve innervates the muscles of the anterior (extensor) compartment of the thigh, including quadriceps femoris and sartorius?
questions.explain: The femoral nerve (L2 to L4) enters the thigh lateral to the femoral artery beneath the inguinal ligament and supplies the anterior thigh compartment muscles (pectineus also receives femoral or obturator branches) plus anterior/medial thigh and leg skin via saphenous nerve.

open.q: Which nerve innervates the quadriceps femoris and anterior compartment of the thigh?

questions.q: Which four muscles make up the quadriceps femoris group?
options: Gracilis, pectineus, adductor longus, and adductor magnus
Rectus femoris, vastus lateralis, vastus medialis, and vastus intermedius
Biceps femoris, semitendinosus, semimembranosus, and sartorius
Tibialis anterior, extensor digitorum longus, fibularis longus, and soleus
questions.explain: Quadriceps femoris consists of rectus femoris (which crosses both hip and knee) and the three vasti muscles (vastus lateralis, vastus medialis, and vastus intermedius), all extending the knee via the patellar tendon/ligament.

open.q: Which four muscles form the quadriceps femoris?
accept: rectus femoris, vastus lateralis, vastus medialis, and vastus intermedius
rectus femoris vastus lateralis vastus medialis vastus intermedius

questions.q: Which muscle forms the lateral boundary of the femoral triangle in the proximal anterior thigh?
questions.explain: The femoral triangle is bounded superiorly by the inguinal ligament, laterally by the medial border of sartorius, and medially by the medial border of adductor longus. Its floor is formed by iliopsoas and pectineus.

open.q: Which muscle forms the lateral border of the femoral triangle?

questions.q: From lateral to medial inside the femoral region/sheath, what is the arrangement of the nerve, artery, vein, and femoral canal?
options: Femoral canal, vein, artery, and nerve
Femoral vein, femoral artery, and femoral nerve
Obturator nerve, profunda femoris artery, and great saphenous vein
Femoral nerve, femoral artery, femoral vein, and femoral canal
questions.explain: Using the NAVL order from lateral to medial: Nerve (femoral nerve outside the sheath), Artery (femoral artery), Vein (femoral vein), and Lymphatics/femoral canal (medial compartment of femoral sheath). A femoral hernia protrudes through the femoral ring/canal.

open.q: What is the lateral-to-medial order of structures from the femoral nerve to the femoral canal?
accept: femoral nerve, femoral artery, femoral vein, and femoral canal

questions.q: Which nerve primarily innervates the adductor compartment of the thigh (including adductor longus, adductor brevis, and gracilis)?
questions.explain: The obturator nerve (L2 to L4) exits through the obturator foramen/canal to innervate most adductors of the medial thigh compartment (adductor longus, adductor brevis, gracilis, obturator externus, and adductor part of adductor magnus).

open.q: Which nerve primarily supplies the adductor muscles of the medial thigh?

questions.q: Why does adductor magnus have a dual nerve supply from both the obturator nerve and the sciatic (tibial) nerve?
options: It has obturator-innervated adductor and tibial-sciatic-innervated hamstring parts
It inserts on the clavicle and scapula
It lacks motor end plates distally
questions.explain: Adductor magnus consists of a medial adductor part innervated by the obturator nerve and a posterior hamstring part (inserting toward the adductor tubercle) innervated by the tibial component of the sciatic nerve.

open.q: Why is adductor magnus innervated by both the obturator nerve and the tibial division of the sciatic nerve?
accept: it combines an adductor part and a hamstring part
it has adductor and hamstring components of different innervation
dual developmental origin as adductor and hamstring portions

questions.q: Which three muscles classically constitute the hamstring group of the posterior thigh?
options: Rectus femoris, vastus lateralis, and sartorius
questions.explain: The hamstrings are biceps femoris, semitendinosus, and semimembranosus; they arise from the ischial tuberosity, cross both hip and knee (extending the hip and flexing the knee), and are innervated by the sciatic nerve.

open.q: Which three muscles make up the hamstring group?

questions.q: Which division of the sciatic nerve supplies the short head of biceps femoris?
questions.explain: While the long head of biceps femoris, semitendinosus, and semimembranosus are supplied by the tibial division of the sciatic nerve, the short head of biceps femoris is supplied by the common fibular (peroneal) division.

open.q: Which division of the sciatic nerve innervates the short head of biceps femoris?

questions.q: Which vessel lies deepest against the popliteal surface of the femur and posterior knee joint capsule within the popliteal fossa?
questions.explain: From superficial to deep in the popliteal fossa, the main neurovascular structures are the tibial nerve (most superficial), popliteal vein, and popliteal artery (deepest against the femur/capsule), making the popliteal artery vulnerable in posterior knee dislocation or supracondylar femoral fracture.

open.q: Which major blood vessel lies deepest in the popliteal fossa against the femur and knee capsule?

questions.q: Which nerve innervates the muscles of the anterior (dorsiflexor) compartment of the leg, including tibialis anterior and extensor hallucis longus?
questions.explain: The deep fibular (peroneal) nerve supplies the anterior leg muscles (tibialis anterior, extensor hallucis longus, extensor digitorum longus, fibularis tertius) that dorsiflex the ankle and extend toes, and supplies skin of the first web space.

open.q: Which nerve supplies the muscles of the anterior compartment of the leg?

questions.q: A patient has a lesion of the common fibular nerve and cannot dorsiflex the ankle or evert the foot, walking with a high-stepping gait to clear the toes. What clinical sign is this?
questions.explain: Loss of anterior and lateral leg compartment innervation (deep and superficial fibular nerves) leads to unopposed plantarflexion/inversion and inability to dorsiflex, producing foot drop and a steppage gait.

open.q: What clinical sign results from loss of ankle dorsiflexion due to fibular nerve injury?

questions.q: Which nerve innervates the lateral compartment muscles of the leg, fibularis (peroneus) longus and fibularis (peroneus) brevis?
questions.explain: The superficial fibular (peroneal) nerve innervates fibularis longus and fibularis brevis in the lateral leg compartment—which evert the foot and weakly plantarflex—and then continues as a cutaneous nerve on the dorsum of the foot.

open.q: Which nerve innervates fibularis longus and fibularis brevis in the lateral leg compartment?

questions.q: Which nerve innervates the muscles of the posterior (plantarflexor) compartment of the leg, including gastrocnemius, soleus, and tibialis posterior?
questions.explain: The tibial nerve (branch of the sciatic nerve) supplies all superficial and deep posterior leg muscles (gastrocnemius, soleus, plantaris, popliteus, tibialis posterior, flexor digitorum longus, and flexor hallucis longus), enabling plantarflexion of the ankle and flexion of the toes.

open.q: Which nerve supplies the muscles of the posterior compartment of the leg?

questions.q: Why is soleus considered an important postural and venous-return muscle of the calf during standing?
options: Its slow-twitch fibres stabilise the ankle; contraction aids venous return
It dorsiflexes and everts the foot
It attaches to the patella and femur
It is supplied by the obturator nerve
questions.explain: Soleus lies deep to gastrocnemius, arises from tibia and fibula (not femur), and contains abundant slow-twitch fibers that help steady the leg over the ankle while acting as a calf muscle pump for venous return.

open.q: How does soleus contribute to posture and venous return in the leg?
accept: it stabilizes the ankle against forward sway and pumps blood in deep calf veins
postural ankle stabilization and calf muscle pump for venous return
resists forward sway at the ankle and assists venous return
slow-twitch postural support and calf venous pumping

questions.q: A runner feels a sudden sharp snap in the posterior lower leg while pushing off sprinting and has a palpable gap in the thick tendon inserting on the calcaneus with inability to actively plantarflex strongly. Which tendon is ruptured?
questions.explain: The calcaneal (Achilles) tendon is the common tendon of gastrocnemius and soleus inserting onto the posterior calcaneus; rupture impairs strong plantarflexion and produces a palpable defect and positive Simmonds/Thompson test.

open.q: Which tendon inserts onto the calcaneus and typically ruptures during sudden push-off in running or jumping?

questions.q: Which nerve can be palpated alongside the dorsalis pedis artery on the dorsum of the foot lateral to the tendon of extensor hallucis longus?
questions.explain: The dorsalis pedis artery (continuation of the anterior tibial artery) runs on the dorsum of the foot with the deep fibular nerve immediately lateral to it, typically lateral to extensor hallucis longus tendon.

open.q: Which nerve runs alongside the dorsalis pedis artery on the dorsum of the foot?

questions.q: Which two terminal branches does the tibial nerve divide into behind/beneath the medial malleolus in the tarsal tunnel?
options: Lateral femoral cutaneous and genitofemoral nerves
Medial plantar and lateral plantar nerves
questions.explain: The tibial nerve passes posterior to the medial malleolus under the flexor retinaculum (tarsal tunnel) and divides into the medial plantar nerve and lateral plantar nerve to supply sole muscles and skin.

open.q: Into which two nerves does the tibial nerve bifurcate near the medial malleolus/tarsal tunnel?
accept: medial plantar and lateral plantar nerves

questions.q: How does the medial plantar nerve compare in territory to the median nerve of the hand?
options: It supplies all plantar skin and every intrinsic foot muscle
It is purely sensory and has no motor branches
It supplies only the fifth toe and lateral sole
It supplies the medial sole and medial 3½ digits, plus four intrinsic muscles
questions.explain: The medial plantar nerve is analogous to the median nerve in the hand, supplying cutaneous innervation to the medial plantar foot and first three and a half toes plus motor supply to abductor hallucis, flexor digitorum brevis, flexor hallucis brevis, and the first lumbrical.

open.q: Which muscles and skin regions of the sole are supplied by the medial plantar nerve?
accept: skin of medial sole and medial three and a half digits plus abductor hallucis, fdb, fhb, and first lumbrical
medial sole/toes skin and abductor hallucis, flexor digitorum brevis, flexor hallucis brevis, first lumbrical

questions.q: Which bone forms the keystone (highest arch point) of the medial longitudinal arch of the foot?
questions.explain: The medial longitudinal arch is higher and more resilient than the lateral arch and is formed by calcaneus, talus, navicular, cuneiforms, and the first three metatarsals, with the talus acting as its keystone.

open.q: Which bone serves as the keystone of the medial longitudinal arch of the foot?

questions.q: Which ligament plays a critical role in supporting the head of the talus and maintaining the medial longitudinal arch of the foot?
questions.explain: The plantar calcaneonavicular (spring) ligament spans from the sustentaculum tali of the calcaneus to the plantar surface of the navicular, supporting the head of the talus and helping maintain the medial longitudinal arch.

open.q: Which ligament supports the head of the talus and helps uphold the medial longitudinal arch?

questions.q: Which tendon passes obliquely across the sole of the foot in a fibrous tunnel to insert onto the base of the first metatarsal and medial cuneiform, helping support the arches?
questions.explain: The fibularis (peroneus) longus tendon winds around the lateral malleolus/cuboid and crosses the plantar foot obliquely to attach to the base of the first metatarsal and medial cuneiform, helping maintain the transverse and longitudinal arches.

open.q: Which tendon crosses the sole of the foot to the first metatarsal and medial cuneiform?

questions.q: Which strong iliofemoral ligament on the anterior aspect of the hip joint prevents excessive hyperextension of the thigh during standing?
questions.explain: The inverted-Y-shaped iliofemoral ligament reinforces the anterior hip joint capsule and strongly resists hyperextension of the hip, allowing upright standing with minimal muscle effort.

open.q: Which anterior hip ligament limits hyperextension of the hip joint?

questions.q: Which intracapsular cruciate ligament of the knee prevents anterior displacement of the tibia relative to the femur?
questions.explain: The anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) extends from the anterior intercondylar area of the tibia posterolaterally to the medial aspect of the lateral femoral condyle, restraining anterior translation of the tibia on the femur.

open.q: Which knee ligament prevents anterior sliding of the tibia relative to the femur?

questions.q: A footballer sustains a severe valgus force to the lateral knee while the foot is planted, tearing the medial collateral ligament, medial meniscus, and anterior cruciate ligament. What classic combination of injuries is this?
questions.explain: The unhappy (O'Donoghue) triad classically involves injury to the tibial (medial) collateral ligament, medial meniscus (attached to the MCL), and anterior cruciate ligament after a valgus/rotational knee blow.

open.q: What is the combined injury of the medial collateral ligament, medial meniscus, and anterior cruciate ligament called?

questions.q: How do the C-shaped medial meniscus and more circular lateral meniscus function inside the knee joint?
options: They attach the patella directly to the fibular head
They secrete synovial fluid only during sleep
They improve joint congruency and distribute load across the tibial plateau
They act as the primary motor extensors of the knee
questions.explain: The menisci are fibrocartilaginous wedges on the tibial plateaus that increase conformity with the rounded femoral condyles, aid lubrication, and distribute compressive forces across the knee.

open.q: What are the main mechanical roles of the menisci in the knee joint?
accept: improving articular congruency and distributing load or shock
deepening tibial plateaus and absorbing shock
cushioning and increasing congruency between femur and tibia

questions.q: Which muscle unlocks the extended knee joint by laterally rotating the femur on a planted tibia (or medially rotating the tibia on the femur)?
questions.explain: At the end of knee extension, slight medial rotation of the femur on the tibia locks the joint; popliteus contracts to laterally rotate the femur on the fixed tibia (or medially rotate the tibia in non-weight-bearing), unlocking the knee to initiate flexion.

open.q: Which muscle unlocks the knee joint to initiate flexion?

questions.q: Why is the medial (tibial) collateral ligament more prone to injury than the lateral (fibular) collateral ligament during a valgus blow to the knee?
options: It attaches to the medial meniscus and resists valgus stress
It is separated from the capsule by popliteus
It lies within the ankle joint
questions.explain: The medial collateral ligament is a broad flat band blending with the joint capsule and medial meniscus that resists valgus forces, whereas the lateral collateral ligament is a rounded cord separated from the lateral meniscus and capsule.

open.q: Why is the medial collateral ligament commonly injured by valgus stress at the knee?
accept: it is a broad band attached to the capsule and medial meniscus resisting valgus forces
it resists valgus forces and blends with the capsule and medial meniscus
broad ligament blended with capsule and medial meniscus

questions.q: Which movements occur predominantly at the subtalar (talocalcaneal) and transverse tarsal joints rather than the talocrural (ankle) joint?
options: Inversion and eversion of the foot
Flexion and extension of the hip
Pronation and supination of the radius
questions.explain: The talocrural (ankle) joint mainly performs dorsiflexion and plantarflexion, whereas inversion (turning sole medially) and eversion (turning sole laterally) occur largely at the subtalar and transverse tarsal joints.

open.q: Which movements of the foot occur mainly at the subtalar and transverse tarsal joints?

questions.q: Where does the great saphenous vein ascend relative to the medial malleolus before traveling up the medial leg and thigh to drain into the femoral vein?
questions.explain: The great saphenous vein is the longest vein in the body and passes consistently anterior to the medial malleolus, ascending along the medial leg and thigh before piercing the saphenous opening to enter the femoral vein.

open.q: In what relation to the medial malleolus does the great saphenous vein pass at the ankle?
accept: in front of the medial malleolus

questions.q: Where does the small saphenous vein typically empty into the deep venous system?
options: Into the external iliac vein at the groin
Into the great saphenous vein at the ankle
Into the popliteal vein in the popliteal fossa
questions.explain: The small saphenous vein arises on the lateral foot, passes posterior to the lateral malleolus, ascends along the posterior leg, and pierces the popliteal fascia to drain into the popliteal vein.

open.q: Into which deep vein does the small saphenous vein typically drain in the popliteal fossa?

questions.q: Which major branch of the femoral artery arises in the femoral triangle and provides the principal arterial supply to the thigh muscles and femur?
options: Deep artery of the thigh (profunda femoris artery)
questions.explain: The deep artery of the thigh (profunda femoris) branches from the posterolateral femoral artery in the femoral triangle and gives off medial and lateral circumflex femoral arteries plus perforating arteries to supply the thigh and proximal femur.

open.q: Which major branch of the femoral artery supplies most of the muscles of the thigh and the femur?

questions.q: Why does the femoral artery become the popliteal artery as it passes through the adductor hiatus of adductor magnus?
options: It passes through the adductor hiatus and becomes the popliteal artery
It divides into internal and external iliac arteries
It crosses the inguinal ligament here
It loses its tunica media in the fossa
questions.explain: As the femoral artery exits the adductor canal through the adductor hiatus in the tendinous insertion of adductor magnus, it enters the popliteal fossa and is termed the popliteal artery.

open.q: What anatomical event marks the transition of the femoral artery into the popliteal artery?
accept: passing through the adductor hiatus into the popliteal fossa
exiting the adductor canal through the adductor hiatus
passing through the opening in adductor magnus

questions.q: At the inferior border of popliteus, the popliteal artery bifurcates into which two arteries?
options: Anterior tibial and posterior tibial arteries
questions.explain: At the inferior margin of popliteus, the popliteal artery divides into the anterior tibial artery (which passes anteriorly above the interosseous membrane) and the posterior tibial artery (which continues posteriorly and gives off the fibular artery).

open.q: Into which two arteries does the popliteal artery divide at the inferior border of popliteus?
accept: anterior tibial and posterior tibial arteries

questions.q: How do perforating veins connect the superficial and deep venous systems of the lower limb?
options: They carry blood from deep veins to superficial veins through the deep fascia
They pierce deep fascia and direct blood from superficial to deep veins
They run inside bone marrow and have no valves
They connect the femoral artery directly to the great saphenous vein
questions.explain: Perforating (perforator) veins pass through the deep fascia between superficial and deep veins; their valves normally direct flow from superficial veins into deep veins, aided by the calf muscle pump. Valve incompetence can cause venous hypertension and varicosities.

open.q: In which direction do valves in lower limb perforating veins normally direct blood flow?
accept: from superficial veins into deep veins
inward from superficial to deep veins

questions.q: Which group of lymph nodes in the lower limb receives superficial lymph from most of the lower limb (excluding the posterolateral calf/small saphenous territory), perineum, and inferior anterior abdominal wall?
questions.explain: Superficial inguinal lymph nodes lie in the subcutaneous tissue below the inguinal ligament and receive superficial lymph from the lower limb (along the great saphenous vein), lower anterior abdominal wall below the umbilicus, buttocks, and perineum/external genitalia.

open.q: Which lymph nodes receive superficial lymphatic drainage from most of the lower limb and lower anterior abdominal wall?

questions.q: Why does the angle of inclination of the femoral neck (typically about 120 to 135 degrees in adults) benefit lower limb biomechanics?
options: It places the femoral shaft laterally, improving the abductors' lever arm
It removes the need for femoral-head cartilage
questions.explain: The angulation of the femoral neck positions the shaft laterally away from the hip joint, giving hip abductors a mechanical lever arm to balance the pelvis and allowing the femur to swing past the pelvis.

open.q: How does the angulation of the femoral neck aid hip biomechanics?
accept: it offsets the shaft laterally to increase abductor lever arm and allow limb clearance
increases mechanical leverage for hip abductors and clears the pelvis during swing
offsets the femoral shaft from the hip joint

questions.q: Which muscle of the medial thigh is long and strap-like, originates from the inferior pubic ramus/body of pubis, and inserts onto the proximal medial tibia as part of the pes anserinus?
questions.explain: Gracilis is the most superficial and medial muscle of the adductor group; it adducts the thigh, flexes the leg, and contributes to the pes anserinus tendon on the proximal medial tibia alongside sartorius and semitendinosus.

open.q: Which medial thigh muscle contributes to the pes anserinus on the proximal medial tibia?

questions.q: A patient has a posterior dislocation of the hip joint after a dashboard impact to a flexed knee, and examination reveals numbness over the lateral leg/dorsum of the foot with weakened ankle dorsiflexion and plantarflexion. Which nerve is most directly endangered by posterior hip dislocation?
questions.explain: Because the sciatic nerve passes posterior to the hip joint in the lower gluteal region, posterior dislocation of the femoral head can stretch or compress the sciatic nerve, causing motor and sensory deficits in its tibial and/or common fibular territories.

open.q: Which nerve lies posterior to the hip joint and is at risk during posterior hip dislocation?

questions.q: Which is the longest and strongest bone in the human body?
questions.explain: The femur is the longest and strongest bone, transmitting body weight from hip to knee.

open.q: Which is the longest and strongest bone in the body?

questions.q: How many metatarsal bones are in each foot?
questions.explain: Each foot has 5 metatarsals, numbered 1 to 5 from medial to lateral.

open.q: How many metatarsal bones are in one foot?

questions.q: What is the deep fascia of the thigh called?
questions.explain: The fascia lata is the deep fascia enclosing the thigh and sends septa to the femur.

open.q: What is the deep fascia of the thigh called?

questions.q: Which nerve supplies gluteus maximus?
questions.explain: Gluteus maximus is supplied by the inferior gluteal nerve (L5, S1, S2).

open.q: Which nerve supplies gluteus maximus?

questions.q: Which muscle is the chief flexor of the hip?
questions.explain: Iliopsoas (iliacus plus psoas major) is the strongest hip flexor.

open.q: Which muscle is the chief flexor of the hip?

questions.q: Which is the longest muscle in the human body?
questions.explain: Sartorius is the longest muscle, running from ASIS to the medial tibia.

open.q: Which is the longest muscle in the human body?

questions.q: Which nerve passes through the popliteal fossa and divides into tibial and common fibular nerves?
questions.explain: The sciatic nerve ends in the popliteal fossa by dividing into tibial and common fibular nerves.

open.q: Which nerve divides into tibial and common fibular nerves in the popliteal fossa?

questions.q: Which artery is the main continuation of the femoral artery into the popliteal fossa?
questions.explain: The femoral artery becomes the popliteal artery as it passes through the adductor hiatus.

open.q: Which artery continues from the femoral artery into the popliteal fossa?

questions.q: What is the most medial compartment of the femoral sheath called?
questions.explain: The femoral sheath has three compartments; the most medial is the femoral canal, containing lymphatics and the node of Cloquet, and it is the route for femoral hernia.

open.q: What is the most medial compartment of the femoral sheath called?

questions.q: A middle-aged woman presents with a swelling below and lateral to the pubic tubercle that expands on coughing. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explain: A femoral hernia passes through the femoral canal and presents below and lateral to the pubic tubercle, unlike an inguinal hernia which is above and medial.

open.q: Which hernia presents inferior and lateral to the pubic tubercle?

questions.q: Which structure does NOT lie in the adductor (subsartorial) canal?
questions.explain: The adductor canal contains the femoral artery, femoral vein, saphenous nerve, and nerve to vastus medialis; the sciatic nerve lies posterior to the thigh.

questions.q: What is the inferior opening of the adductor canal called?
questions.explain: The adductor hiatus is the opening in the tendinous insertion of adductor magnus through which the femoral vessels pass into the popliteal fossa.

open.q: What is the inferior opening of the adductor canal called?

questions.q: Which three muscles insert together as the pes anserinus on the proximal medial tibia?
questions.explain: The pes anserinus (goose's foot) is formed by sartorius, gracilis, and semitendinosus inserting on the proximal medial tibia.

open.q: Which three muscles form the pes anserinus?

questions.q: A patient has pain over the proximal medial tibia just below the knee, worsened by resisted knee flexion and medial rotation. Which structure is inflamed?
questions.explain: Pes anserinus bursitis/tendinopathy causes medial knee pain at the proximal medial tibia, aggravated by flexion and medial rotation.

open.q: Which structure at the proximal medial tibia is inflamed in pes anserinus bursitis?

questions.q: What type of joint is the sacroiliac joint?
questions.explain: The sacroiliac joint is a strong synovial joint anteriorly with a symphyseal (secondary cartilaginous) component, held by very strong ligaments.

open.q: What type of joint is the sacroiliac joint?

questions.q: Which ligament is the strongest of the sacroiliac ligaments and resists nutation of the sacrum?
questions.explain: The interosseous sacroiliac ligament is the strongest, filling the space between the sacrum and ilium and limiting sacral nutation.

open.q: Which is the strongest of the sacroiliac ligaments?

questions.q: What is the medial ligament of the ankle joint called?
questions.explain: The deltoid (medial collateral) ligament is a strong triangular ligament attaching the medial malleolus to the talus, calcaneus, and navicular.

open.q: What is the medial ligament of the ankle joint called?

questions.q: A footballer twists his ankle in inversion, causing the most commonly injured ankle ligament to tear. Which ligament is this?
questions.explain: The anterior talofibular ligament is the most commonly injured ankle ligament in inversion sprains.

open.q: Which ankle ligament is most commonly injured in an inversion sprain?

questions.q: Which lateral ankle ligament lies below the other two and attaches to the calcaneus?
questions.explain: The calcaneofibular ligament runs from the lateral malleolus to the calcaneus and is the second most commonly injured lateral ligament.

open.q: Which lateral ankle ligament attaches the lateral malleolus to the calcaneus?

questions.q: Which structure forms the roof of the tarsal tunnel?
questions.explain: The flexor retinaculum (laciniate ligament) forms the roof of the tarsal tunnel behind the medial malleolus.

open.q: Which structure forms the roof of the tarsal tunnel?

questions.q: A patient has burning pain and numbness of the sole with weakness of toe flexion after ankle swelling. Which syndrome is this?
questions.explain: Tarsal tunnel syndrome results from compression of the tibial nerve behind the medial malleolus, causing sole numbness and weakness of intrinsic foot muscles.

open.q: Which syndrome results from compression of the tibial nerve in the tarsal tunnel?

questions.q: What is the main function of the plantar aponeurosis?
options: Supporting the longitudinal arches of the foot
questions.explain: The plantar aponeurosis is a thick fibrous band that supports the longitudinal arches and protects plantar structures.

open.q: What is the main function of the plantar aponeurosis?

questions.q: A patient has severe heel pain with the first steps in the morning, localized to the medial calcaneal tubercle. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explain: Plantar fasciitis causes medial heel pain worst with first morning steps, due to inflammation at the calcaneal attachment of the plantar fascia.

open.q: Which condition causes medial heel pain worst on first morning steps?

questions.q: Which nerve roots form the femoral nerve?
questions.explain: The femoral nerve arises from the posterior divisions of the anterior rami of L2, L3, and L4.

open.q: Which nerve roots form the femoral nerve?

questions.q: Which nerve roots form the sciatic nerve?
questions.explain: The sciatic nerve arises from the anterior rami of L4 to S3 (L4, L5, S1, S2, S3) via the sacral plexus.

open.q: Which nerve roots form the sciatic nerve?

questions.q: Which nerve roots form the obturator nerve?
questions.explain: The obturator nerve arises from the anterior divisions of the anterior rami of L2, L3, and L4.

open.q: Which nerve roots form the obturator nerve?

questions.q: Which lymph nodes drain the posterolateral calf and receive the small saphenous vein?
questions.explain: Popliteal lymph nodes lie in the popliteal fossa and receive lymph from the posterolateral calf and small saphenous territory.

open.q: Which lymph nodes drain the posterolateral calf?

questions.q: Which lymph nodes lie deep to the fascia lata along the femoral vessels and receive lymph from the glans penis or clitoris?
questions.explain: Deep inguinal nodes lie medial to the femoral vein under the fascia lata and receive lymph from deep structures and the glans penis/clitoris.

open.q: Which lymph nodes lie deep to the fascia lata along the femoral vessels?

questions.q: Which nerve is the terminal sensory branch of the femoral nerve supplying the medial leg and foot?
questions.explain: The saphenous nerve is the terminal sensory branch of the femoral nerve, supplying the medial leg and medial border of the foot.

open.q: Which sensory nerve supplies the medial leg and foot?

questions.q: A patient cannot extend the knee after a femoral nerve injury from a penetrating wound in the femoral triangle. Which muscle group is paralyzed?
questions.explain: The femoral nerve supplies quadriceps femoris; injury causes loss of knee extension and absent knee jerk.

open.q: Which muscle group is paralyzed after femoral nerve injury in the femoral triangle?

questions.q: How does the gait in a unilateral gluteus medius lesion differ from the gait in a bilateral gluteus medius lesion?
options: Unilateral: Trendelenburg lurch; bilateral: waddling gait
Both cause the same waddling gait
Unilateral: foot drop; bilateral: high-stepping gait
questions.explain: Unilateral gluteus medius weakness produces a Trendelenburg lurch to the affected side; bilateral weakness produces a waddling gait.

open.q: What gait pattern results from bilateral gluteus medius weakness?

questions.q: What is the normal Q-angle at the knee in an adult male?
questions.explain: The Q-angle is the angle between the quadriceps pull and the patellar tendon; it is normally about 10–15 degrees in males and slightly larger in females.

open.q: What is the normal Q-angle at the knee in an adult male?

questions.q: A teenage girl has recurrent lateral patellar dislocation. Which factor most predisposes to this?
questions.explain: A large Q-angle (common in females and adolescents) increases lateral pull on the patella, predisposing to lateral dislocation.

open.q: Which biomechanical factor predisposes to lateral patellar dislocation?

questions.q: Which movement of the hip is most strongly limited by the iliofemoral ligament during standing?
questions.explain: The iliofemoral ligament (Y ligament of Bigelow) limits hyperextension of the hip, allowing upright standing with minimal muscle effort.

open.q: Which hip movement is limited by the iliofemoral ligament?

questions.q: A patient has a positive Trendelenburg sign on the right. Which side is the lesion on?
questions.explain: A positive Trendelenburg sign on the right means the right gluteus medius is weak, causing the left pelvis to drop when standing on the right leg.

open.q: A positive Trendelenburg sign on the right indicates weakness of which muscle group?

questions.q: Which muscle forms the floor of the femoral triangle medial to iliopsoas?
questions.explain: The floor of the femoral triangle is formed by iliopsoas laterally and pectineus medially.

open.q: Which muscle forms the medial part of the floor of the femoral triangle?

questions.q: Which artery is the main arterial supply to the head of the femur in adults?
questions.explain: The medial circumflex femoral artery provides most of the blood supply to the femoral head and neck in adults, and its disruption in femoral neck fracture risks avascular necrosis.

open.q: Which artery provides most of the blood supply to the adult femoral head?

questions.q: An elderly patient has a displaced femoral neck fracture. Which complication is most likely due to disruption of the blood supply to the femoral head?
options: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head
questions.explain: Displaced femoral neck fractures disrupt the medial circumflex femoral artery, causing avascular necrosis of the femoral head.

open.q: Which complication of a displaced femoral neck fracture results from loss of blood supply to the femoral head?

questions.q: During a groin operation, a superficial vein is followed as it pierces the fascia lata to join the femoral vein. Through which opening does it pass?
questions.explain: The great saphenous vein pierces the cribriform fascia covering the saphenous opening in the fascia lata to join the femoral vein. The femoral artery and vein do not pass through the saphenous opening.

open.q: Through which opening in the fascia lata does the great saphenous vein enter the femoral vein?

questions.q: A surgeon exposes the saphenous opening in the fascia lata. Which structure forms the thin fascial covering over this opening?
questions.explain: The saphenous opening is covered by cribriform fascia, a perforated part of the superficial fascia lata through which the great saphenous vein and superficial vessels and lymphatics pass.

open.q: What fascia covers the saphenous opening in the fascia lata?

questions.q: A patient crosses one leg over the other and then flexes the knee to bring the ankle toward the opposite thigh. Which long strap-like muscle contributes to these combined movements?
questions.explain: Sartorius flexes, abducts and laterally rotates the thigh at the hip and also flexes the knee. It crosses both the hip and knee joints and is the longest muscle in the body.

open.q: Which muscle flexes, abducts and laterally rotates the thigh while also flexing the knee?

questions.q: A surgeon explores the popliteal fossa from superficial to deep in the midline. Which sequence correctly describes the usual arrangement of its major neurovascular contents?
options: Popliteal artery, popliteal vein, tibial nerve
Tibial nerve, popliteal vein, popliteal artery
Popliteal vein, tibial nerve, popliteal artery
Tibial nerve, popliteal artery, popliteal vein
questions.explain: The usual superficial-to-deep arrangement in the central popliteal fossa is tibial nerve, popliteal vein and popliteal artery. The artery is deepest, lying close to the femur and posterior capsule of the knee joint.

open.q: What is the usual superficial-to-deep order of the tibial nerve, popliteal vein and popliteal artery?
accept: tibial nerve, popliteal vein, popliteal artery

questions.q: A clinician palpates the dorsalis pedis pulse on the dorsum of the foot. This artery is the direct continuation of which vessel after it passes the ankle joint?
questions.explain: The anterior tibial artery crosses the ankle joint and continues onto the dorsum of the foot as the dorsalis pedis artery. The posterior tibial artery passes behind the medial malleolus and divides into the plantar arteries.

open.q: Which leg artery continues onto the dorsum of the foot as the dorsalis pedis artery?

questions.q: A patient has a small area of sensory loss in the cleft between the great toe and second toe after an ankle injury. Which nerve supplies this cutaneous area?
questions.explain: The deep fibular (deep peroneal) nerve supplies the skin in the first dorsal web space between the great toe and second toe. The superficial fibular nerve supplies most of the remaining dorsum of the foot.

open.q: Which nerve supplies sensation to the first dorsal web space of the foot?

questions.q: A vascular surgeon assesses the arterial supply to the plantar foot. Which artery forms most of the plantar arterial arch?
questions.explain: The plantar arterial arch is formed mainly by the lateral plantar artery, which anastomoses with the deep plantar branch of the dorsalis pedis artery. The medial plantar artery is smaller.

open.q: Which plantar artery forms most of the plantar arterial arch?

questions.q: A woman presents with lateral deviation of the great toe at the first metatarsophalangeal joint, accompanied by a prominent medial eminence at the first metatarsal head. What is this deformity called?
questions.explain: Hallux valgus is lateral deviation of the great toe at the first metatarsophalangeal joint, often associated with a medial bony prominence (bunion) at the first metatarsal head.

open.q: What is the term for lateral deviation of the great toe at the first metatarsophalangeal joint?

questions.q: A newborn's foot is fixed in plantarflexion and inversion, with the forefoot adducted. Which congenital deformity does this describe?
questions.explain: Talipes equinovarus (clubfoot) is characterized by an inverted and plantarflexed foot with forefoot adduction. It may involve soft-tissue contractures and bony malalignment.

open.q: Which congenital foot deformity combines plantarflexion, inversion and forefoot adduction?

questions.q: A surgeon requires a tendon graft for reconstructive surgery and considers harvesting the plantaris tendon. Why can this tendon usually be removed without causing major functional loss?
options: It is the primary plantarflexor of the ankle
Its contribution to lower-limb movement is minor and its function is largely duplicated by other muscles
It is a sensory structure rather than a muscle tendon
It is normally absent in adults
questions.explain: Plantaris is a small, variable muscle with a long slender tendon. Its action is weak and largely redundant with gastrocnemius and soleus, so its tendon can often be harvested as a graft without significant functional disability.

open.q: Why can the plantaris tendon often be harvested for grafting with little functional deficit?
accept: its action is minor and redundant with gastrocnemius and soleus
minor function duplicated by other plantarflexors
it has a minor role in lower-limb movement

questions.q: An athlete's ankle is forced into eversion. The medial ligament is placed under tension and a fracture occurs at the medial malleolus. Which injury pattern is most consistent with this mechanism?
options: Inversion sprain of the lateral ligament
questions.explain: Forced eversion can tension the strong deltoid ligament and avulse the medial malleolus. Continued force may drive the talus laterally and fracture the fibula, producing a Pott fracture-dislocation pattern.

open.q: What ankle fracture-dislocation can follow forceful eversion with injury to the medial malleolus?

questions.q: A child is noted to have genu valgum. In which direction is the tibia deviated relative to the femoral axis?
questions.explain: In genu valgum (knock-knee), the tibia is deviated laterally relative to the femur, increasing the valgus angle at the knee. In genu varum (bow legs), the tibia is deviated medially.

open.q: In genu valgum, in which direction is the tibia deviated relative to the femur?

questions.q: A long-distance runner develops lateral knee pain associated with repetitive flexion and extension. Which structure, formed by the tensor fasciae latae and gluteus maximus fascia, helps stabilise the knee during stance?
questions.explain: The iliotibial tract is a thickened lateral part of the fascia lata receiving fibres from tensor fasciae latae and gluteus maximus. It inserts into the lateral tibial condyle (Gerdy's tubercle) and helps stabilise the knee, particularly during weight-bearing and partial flexion. Repetitive friction or compression near the lateral femoral epicondyle can contribute to iliotibial band syndrome.

questions.q: A patient has difficulty initiating abduction of the thigh and shows a positive Trendelenburg sign after injury to a nerve emerging above piriformis. Which muscle group is primarily denervated?
options: Gluteus maximus and short lateral rotators
Gluteus medius, gluteus minimus and tensor fasciae latae
questions.explain: The superior gluteal nerve supplies gluteus medius, gluteus minimus and tensor fasciae latae. Weakness of the hip abductors causes the pelvis to drop on the unsupported side during single-leg stance (Trendelenburg sign).

open.q: Name the principal muscles supplied by the superior gluteal nerve and state the clinical sign caused by their paralysis.
accept: Gluteus medius, gluteus minimus and tensor fasciae latae; Trendelenburg sign
Gluteus medius and minimus with tensor fasciae latae; pelvic drop on contralateral side

questions.q: During arthroscopy, a surgeon notes that the anterior cruciate ligament is intracapsular but lies outside the synovial cavity. Which description best explains this relationship?
options: It is completely surrounded by synovial fluid
It is excluded from the synovial cavity by a reflection of the synovial membrane
It lies outside the fibrous capsule
It is located within the prepatellar bursa
questions.explain: The cruciate ligaments are intracapsular but extrasynovial. The synovial membrane reflects around them, excluding them from the synovial cavity while they remain within the fibrous capsule.

open.q: Describe the relationship of the cruciate ligaments to the fibrous capsule and synovial cavity of the knee.
accept: Within the fibrous capsule but excluded from the synovial cavity

questions.q: As the knee approaches full extension in a weight-bearing person, the femur rotates medially on the fixed tibia. Which mechanism is being described?
options: Lateral rotation of the femur during flexion
Anterior translation of the tibia by quadriceps
questions.explain: In the final degrees of weight-bearing knee extension, the femur rotates medially on the fixed tibia (or the tibia laterally on the femur in open-chain extension). This screw-home mechanism tightens the collateral and cruciate ligaments and stabilises the extended knee. Popliteus initiates unlocking.

open.q: Explain the screw-home mechanism of the knee during terminal extension in a weight-bearing limb.
accept: Medial rotation of femur on fixed tibia in closed chain; lateral rotation of tibia in open chain
Terminal extension produces rotation that locks the knee

questions.q: A femoral hernia passes through the femoral ring. Which structure normally occupies the medial compartment of the femoral sheath and may be displaced by the hernia?
options: Femoral canal containing lymphatics and loose connective tissue
questions.explain: The femoral sheath encloses the femoral artery, femoral vein and femoral canal. The femoral canal is the medial compartment and contains loose connective tissue, lymphatics and the deep inguinal node (Cloquet). The femoral nerve lies outside the sheath.

open.q: What occupies the medial compartment of the femoral sheath, and which major nerve lies outside the sheath?
accept: Femoral canal with lymphatics and loose connective tissue; femoral nerve lies outside
Femoral canal; femoral nerve is outside the sheath

questions.q: A penetrating wound damages the profunda femoris artery near its origin. Which major branch normally arises from it to contribute to the cruciate anastomosis?
options: Descending branch of lateral circumflex femoral artery
questions.explain: The profunda femoris (deep artery of the thigh) commonly gives rise to the medial and lateral circumflex femoral arteries and perforating branches. The medial circumflex femoral artery contributes to the cruciate anastomosis and is an important source of blood to the femoral head in adults.

open.q: Name two circumflex femoral branches of the profunda femoris artery and identify which is especially important to the adult femoral head.
accept: Medial and lateral circumflex femoral arteries; medial circumflex femoral artery
Medial circumflex femoral artery supplies much of femoral head

questions.q: In the central part of the popliteal fossa, which sequence describes the structures from superficial to deep?
options: Popliteal artery, popliteal vein, tibial nerve
Tibial nerve, popliteal vein, popliteal artery
Popliteal vein, tibial nerve, popliteal artery
Tibial nerve, popliteal artery, popliteal vein
questions.explain: The usual superficial-to-deep arrangement is tibial nerve, popliteal vein and popliteal artery. The artery is deepest, lying close to the posterior surface of the knee joint capsule.

open.q: Arrange the tibial nerve, popliteal vein and popliteal artery from superficial to deep in the popliteal fossa.
accept: Tibial nerve, popliteal vein, popliteal artery

questions.q: A deep laceration in the anterior compartment of the leg is followed by foot drop and loss of sensation in the first dorsal web space. Which nerve is most likely injured?
questions.explain: The deep fibular (peroneal) nerve supplies the anterior compartment muscles responsible for dorsiflexion and provides cutaneous sensation to the first dorsal web space. Injury causes foot drop and sensory loss in that small area.

open.q: Which nerve lesion produces foot drop with sensory loss in the first dorsal web space?

questions.q: A patient with weakness of the muscle that passes beneath the foot from the lateral to medial side has difficulty maintaining the transverse arch. Which muscle is most likely affected?
questions.explain: Fibularis longus tendon crosses the sole obliquely in a groove on the cuboid and inserts on the medial cuneiform and base of the first metatarsal. It helps support the transverse arch and also everts and plantarflexes the foot.

open.q: Which muscle tendon crosses the sole to insert on the medial cuneiform and base of the first metatarsal, helping support the transverse arch?

questions.q: A varicose vein procedure targets the great saphenous vein. At which site does this vein normally enter the deep venous system?
options: Behind the lateral malleolus into the popliteal vein
Through the saphenous opening into the femoral vein
Through the adductor hiatus into the popliteal vein
Behind the medial malleolus into the posterior tibial vein
questions.explain: The great saphenous vein ascends anterior to the medial malleolus and along the medial leg and thigh, then passes through the saphenous opening to join the femoral vein just inferior to the inguinal ligament.

open.q: Describe the termination of the great saphenous vein.
accept: It passes through the saphenous opening to join the femoral vein
Joins femoral vein just inferior to inguinal ligament

questions.q: An elderly patient sustains an intracapsular fracture of the femoral neck. Which vessel is most important for the blood supply to the adult femoral head and is therefore at risk?
options: Obturator artery via the acetabular branch
Medial circumflex femoral artery via retinacular branches
Inferior gluteal artery via muscular branches
Lateral circumflex femoral artery via descending branch
questions.explain: In adults, retinacular branches of the medial circumflex femoral artery provide the principal blood supply to the femoral head. Intracapsular femoral neck fractures can disrupt these vessels and cause avascular necrosis.

open.q: Which artery provides the principal retinacular blood supply to the adult femoral head and is endangered in intracapsular femoral neck fractures?
accept: Retinacular branches of medial circumflex femoral artery

questions.q: A patient undergoes surgery in the middle third of the thigh. Which nerve normally traverses the adductor canal with the femoral vessels but leaves it by piercing the roof before reaching the medial knee?
questions.explain: The saphenous nerve, a sensory branch of the femoral nerve, accompanies the femoral artery through the adductor canal and pierces the subsartorial fascia to become superficial. It does not pass through the adductor hiatus with the vessels.

open.q: A patient undergoes surgery in the middle third of the thigh. Which nerve normally traverses the adductor canal with the femoral vessels but leaves it by piercing the roof before reaching the medial knee?

questions.q: A patient has a proximal hamstring injury involving the long head of biceps femoris and semitendinosus. Which part of the sciatic nerve supplies these muscles?
questions.explain: The hamstring muscles, including the long head of biceps femoris, semitendinosus and semimembranosus, are supplied by the tibial division of the sciatic nerve. The short head of biceps femoris is supplied by the common fibular division.

open.q: A patient has a proximal hamstring injury involving the long head of biceps femoris and semitendinosus. Which part of the sciatic nerve supplies these muscles?
accept: Tibial division of the sciatic nerve

questions.q: A melanoma on the lateral side of the foot spreads first to which group of lymph nodes in the usual superficial drainage pathway?
questions.explain: Most superficial lymphatics accompanying the small saphenous vein from the lateral foot and posterolateral leg drain first to popliteal nodes. Efferents then pass to deep inguinal nodes.

open.q: A melanoma on the lateral side of the foot spreads first to which group of lymph nodes in the usual superficial drainage pathway?

questions.q: A patient has sensory loss over the medial side of the leg and medial malleolus after a lumbar root lesion. Which dermatome is most likely involved?
questions.explain: The L4 dermatome classically includes the medial leg and medial malleolus. L2 is mainly anterior upper thigh, L5 includes the dorsum of the foot and great toe, and S1 includes the lateral foot.

open.q: A patient has sensory loss over the medial side of the leg and medial malleolus after a lumbar root lesion. Which dermatome is most likely involved?

questions.q: An adolescent presents with limp and referred knee pain. Radiographs show displacement through the proximal femoral growth plate. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.explain: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis is displacement of the femoral head epiphysis relative to the femoral neck through the growth plate, usually in adolescents. Hip pathology may present as thigh or knee pain, so the hip must be examined in a patient with unexplained knee pain.

open.q: An adolescent presents with limp and referred knee pain. Radiographs show displacement through the proximal femoral growth plate. Which diagnosis is most likely?

questions.q: During a posterior hip approach, the surgeon identifies the sciatic nerve emerging inferior to piriformis. Which landmark is commonly used to estimate its position in the gluteal region?
options: Midpoint between the ischial tuberosity and greater trochanter
Midpoint between anterior superior iliac spine and pubic tubercle
Line joining the two anterior superior iliac spines
Point midway between the sacral promontory and coccyx
questions.explain: The sciatic nerve usually emerges below piriformis and descends deep to gluteus maximus. In the gluteal region, its surface projection is commonly described near the midpoint between the ischial tuberosity and greater trochanter; this is a useful but approximate landmark.

open.q: During a posterior hip approach, the surgeon identifies the sciatic nerve emerging inferior to piriformis. Which landmark is commonly used to estimate its position in the gluteal region?
accept: Midpoint between the ischial tuberosity and greater trochanter

questions.q: A patient sustains a blow to the lateral side of the knee while the foot is fixed. Which ligament is most likely stressed by a valgus force?
questions.explain: A valgus force opens the medial side of the knee and stresses the tibial collateral ligament. A varus force stresses the fibular collateral ligament.

open.q: A patient sustains a blow to the lateral side of the knee while the foot is fixed. Which ligament is most likely stressed by a valgus force?

questions.q: A patient cannot plantarflex the ankle effectively and has lost sensation over most of the sole after a deep injury posterior to the medial malleolus. Which nerve is most likely damaged?
questions.explain: The tibial nerve passes behind the medial malleolus within the tarsal tunnel and gives rise to medial and lateral plantar nerves. It supplies the posterior compartment of the leg and most intrinsic plantar muscles; injury can impair plantarflexion and plantar sensation.

open.q: A patient cannot plantarflex the ankle effectively and has lost sensation over most of the sole after a deep injury posterior to the medial malleolus. Which nerve is most likely damaged?

questions.q: After an intramuscular injection into the gluteal region, a patient develops foot drop and weakness of knee flexion. Which structure was most likely injured by an incorrectly placed injection?
questions.explain: The sciatic nerve passes deep to gluteus maximus and is vulnerable to an improperly placed gluteal injection. Injury can affect hamstring function and muscles below the knee, producing foot drop.

open.q: Which major nerve may be injured by an incorrectly placed gluteal intramuscular injection?

questions.q: A patient has a posterior knee injury with weak plantarflexion and sensory loss over much of the sole. Which terminal branch of the sciatic nerve is most likely damaged?
questions.explain: The tibial nerve supplies the posterior compartment of the leg and most intrinsic plantar foot muscles through its plantar branches. Injury can impair plantarflexion and plantar sensation.

open.q: Which terminal branch of the sciatic nerve supplies the posterior leg compartment and plantar foot?
